Compute Neighborhood Quality Metrics

Source: R/helpers.R
qc_neighborhoods.Rd

Reports the effective neighbourhood size at one or more bandwidths, so you can tell whether a bandwidth is usable before interpreting a curve computed with it.

qc_neighborhoods(
  coords,
  h,
  kernel = c("gaussian", "uniform", "exponential"),
  distance = c("euclidean", "manhattan", "minkowski"),
  eps = 0,
  p = 2
)

Arguments

coords

Coordinates matrix (N x 2)

h

Bandwidth, or a vector of bandwidths. A vector previously recycled silently against the distance matrix and returned meaningless numbers.

kernel

Character. "gaussian", "uniform" or "exponential", matching what you will pass to multiScaleAC. It must match, or the diagnostic describes a different model from the one you fit.

distance

Character. "euclidean", "manhattan" or "minkowski".

eps

Weight threshold, matching multiScaleAC.

p

Order of the Minkowski distance, matching multiScaleAC.

Value

A data frame with one row per bandwidth:

h

The bandwidth

mean_neighbors

Mean kernel row sum, the effective neighbourhood size

sd_neighbors

Standard deviation of the row sums

min_neighbors

Smallest row sum

max_neighbors

Largest row sum

isolated_cells

Cells whose row sum is exactly zero

percent_isolated

The same as a percentage

saturation

Mean row sum divided by N. Values near 1 mean the kernel is effectively constant and the bandwidth is too large to be informative.

Details

What "effective" means. For the Gaussian kernel every pair has a non-zero weight, so counting neighbours within a hard radius describes a different model from the one being fitted. This function reports the kernel row sum, which is the weight actually carried, and equals a plain neighbour count only for the uniform kernel. The previous version applied a hard distance <= h cutoff regardless of kernel, so under the default Gaussian setting it could never report an isolated cell.

Interpretation: a mean row sum close to N means the kernel is saturated, every cell is effectively everyone's neighbour, and Moran's I will collapse toward zero whatever the biology. A mean near zero means almost no cell has a neighbour carrying weight and the statistic is unstable or undefined.

Examples

data(ccRCCExample)
coords <- as.matrix(ccRCCExample[1:1500, c("x", "y")])

# Coordinates are in millimetres. Sensible bandwidths, and one far too large:
qc_neighborhoods(coords, h = c(0.01, 0.05, 0.25, 25))
#>       h mean_neighbors sd_neighbors min_neighbors max_neighbors isolated_cells
#> 1  0.01        6.27293   2.04938793  2.896103e-02      12.15022              0
#> 2  0.05      141.09225  44.06580726  1.103950e+01     205.97612              0
#> 3  0.25     1086.03188 118.92095661  5.266455e+02    1257.56130              0
#> 4 25.00     1498.94445   0.02160196  1.498812e+03    1498.97222              0
#>   percent_isolated saturation
#> 1                0     0.0042
#> 2                0     0.0941
#> 3                0     0.7240
#> 4                0     0.9993
# The last row has saturation near 1 -- that bandwidth cannot detect anything.
